nodes.carry_quote: “But it was my intention to hunt him out in all his hiding-places and show him for what he is and always has been.” — Elias Canetti, Crowds and Power, Epilogue, ‘The End of the Survivor’ (tr. Carol Stewart)
prompts: 1. The Epilogue says the survivor must be hunted 'in all his hiding-places'. The week found Canetti's own books to be the densest source of commentary on him. Is an author who explains his own first book acting as survivor of it? Write a page that tests the analogy and then breaks it.

2. Edge 15: Urteil as opinion, verdict, judgment. Pick a word in your own work that a translator would have to choose between three English nouns for, and write the three sentences. Which would a hostile reader prefer?

3. The misreading in section 3 predicts that ideas lose their names as they spread. Find one of your own coinages in someone else's text (or imagine it there) and decide what you would count as credit.

nodes.title: Shadow — Kathy Acker, day 1: The Card Says Alexandria
nodes.thread: Day 1 (the author). Great Expectations (1178, 1982) read from its EPUB; seven sources checked against texts in Scribrarium: Dickens's Great Expectations (opening sentence: 'family' cut, Pip → Peter; end of ch. XIX; Jaggers's card 'just out of Smithfield' → 'just outside Alexandria'), Edwin Drood (opium den, Rosa Bud; 'much credit' → 'MasterCharge cards') and Bleak House (fog → 'Red everywhere') in 8747; Guyotat, Eden Eden Eden (4776; Acker 1982 predates Fox's 1995 English); Flaubert's letters (5751: 'die at eighty' → 'die at sixty'); Keats, Eve of St. Agnes st. 1 (8742); Colette, The Pure and the Impure (3267, p. 117: dialogue verbatim, Renée given a new answer). Not checkable here: Story of O, Proust's Time Regained (sentence printed twice, names swapped), Propertius, Jonson, Melville's Redburn, Princesse de Clèves. Finding: she changes the smallest unit (one word, name, number, answer) and leaves the rest standing, so the change is the signature. Edges run outward (6 Rewrites, 1 Quotes). Mentions: 263 books (245 exact 'Kathy Acker' + 18 by surname, hand-checked); plugin search timed out, captured by read-only substring scan of full-text-search.db.
nodes.carry_quote: “It’s a common belief that something exists when it’s part of a narrative.” — Kathy Acker, Great Expectations, Part Two, ‘Day’
prompts: 1. Acker changes eighty to sixty in Flaubert's sentence. Take a sentence you admire and change one number in it so that it becomes about you. Does the change make it yours, or only make it wrong?

2. The Proust passage is printed twice, names changed, with nothing between. Write a paragraph of your own and then its double with different proper names. Where does the meaning go when only the names move?

3. 'One text must subvert (the meaning of) another text until there's only background music.' Goal, or a description of what happens to any commonplace book kept long enough? Test it against your own Lexicon.

nodes.title: Shadow — Kathy Acker, day 2: The Room No One Else Wants
nodes.thread: Day 2 (who quotes her). A 7-word-shingle comparison of all 259 non-own Mentions books against Acker's four library books (1176, 1177, 1178, 10951) located verbatim quotation; three books read and collated: McCarthy, Typewriters, Bombs, Jellyfish (4206; 'Kathy Acker's Infidel Heteroglossia', 23 runs/526 words from four Acker books); Bal, Narratology 4th ed. 2017 (9197; 154-word run, the hexagon bedroom, p. 102); Campbell, Poetic Revolutionaries (5541; 58 runs/1,728 words). Finding: the field quotes a narrow band of Blood and Guts (Grove pp. 34–37): Bal and Campbell both reproduce Janey's hexagon bedroom in full citing p. 36 (FTS: no other book in the library has it); McCarthy and Bal both quote the 'rotgut' abortions sentence. Quoting her, each critic changes the smallest unit, the scale Acker worked at: McCarthy this→the world, 'We all'→'We', anything→everything, as if→as though, Bolitho→Boitho; Bal drops 'real', for just→just for; Campbell My room→My bedroom, +'kind of', −'red', −'that', −'is'. Witnesses check each other (Bal's Grove 1984 hexagon matches the Penguin 2017 EPUB exactly). McCarthy attributes to Empire of the Senseless lines ('Sex is public … Go over this threshold with me.') that stand in GE Part Three 'Inside' (here→there); Empire not in library, so open question. Campbell's chapter title 'Kathy Acker or Catheter the Hack' comes from Acker's own renaming in Don Quixote (not in library). Edges 36–43, all Quotes, all inward.
nodes.carry_quote: “My room is the room no one else in the world wants.” — Kathy Acker, Blood and Guts in High School, ‘Inside High School’ / ‘The Scorpions’ (Grove p. 36)
prompts: 1. Campbell writes 'My bedroom is the room' where Acker wrote 'My room is the room', and a page later builds an argument on 'leopard coat' against 'leopard skin coat'. Write a page on attention: what makes a reader exact about one word and careless about the next?
2. McCarthy proposes 'a powerful infidel heteroglossia' as a catalogue description. Write the catalogue card for Great Expectations that a librarian following him would file, with subject headings.
3. Bal asks whether the hexagon passage turns iterative through one sentence. Find a passage in your own work where a single sentence changes how often everything before it has happened.

nodes.title: Shadow — Kathy Acker, day 3: The Dissent Is Absent
nodes.thread: Day 3 (who argues with her). No book in the library argues against Acker in its own voice; the dissent survives only as quotation inside her defenders, each objection quoted in order to be refuted, and none of the source texts is in the catalogue: McHale 1992 ('pointless', Jameson's 'blank parody') in Nicol, Cambridge Introduction to Postmodern Fiction (6623, pp. 158–162); Niall Lucy 2000 ('bad writing rather than transgressive writing') in Robinson, Shift Linguals (5612, p. 165); an unnamed LRB reviewer ('Ackerish wailing and stamping') in Zambreno, Appendix Project (3591). McHale himself is on the shelf in the Routledge Companion to Experimental Literature (708, 2012, ch. 11 § III): the same Gibson/Acker passage is now 'an ontological flicker'; the 1992 verdict is neither repeated nor retracted. The defence is weakest where day 1 was strongest: Nicol calls the borrowing 'almost deliberately clumsy and slapdash' and says the GE opening differs from Dickens only by Pip→Peter ('family' is also cut); writes 'Jenny' for Janey and 'Her Pip' (no Pip in Acker's GE). McHale says Acker adds 'oddly irrelevant details of her own', but 'A construct.' is Gibson's noun from two sentences later (Neuromancer 9341, ch. 5), and left wrist→right wrist is again the smallest unit. Robinson's BG quotation drifts (comma added, 'and' dropped). Jameson's 'sense of humour' (Cultural Turn 22) → 'sense of humor' (Norton 3266) → 'its humor' (Butler in Norton). Edges 44–48.
nodes.carry_quote: “But, at the risk of sounding glib, the pointlessness is actually the point.” — Bran Nicol, The Cambridge Introduction to Postmodern Fiction, ch. 6, p. 160
prompts: 1. Nicol says the borrowing is 'almost deliberately clumsy and slapdash'; day 1 found eighty changed to sixty. Write a page on the difference between a careless copy and a copy that wants to look careless. What would count as evidence for either?

2. McHale moved from 'pointless' to 'an ontological flicker' without repeating or retracting the first verdict. Pick a judgement you once wrote and later reversed. Write the paragraph in which the reversal is visible only to someone who has read both.

3. The dissent against Acker on these shelves exists only inside her defenders. Choose a writer you admire and list the objections to them you know only from the people who answered them. Which of those objections have you never read in their own words?

nodes.title: Shadow — Kathy Acker, day 4: The Sentence Was Sartre's
nodes.thread: Day 4 (who rewrites, edits, introduces her), both directions. OUTWARD: the 'My Death' section of My Death My Life by Pier Paolo Pasolini (in Literal Madness, 1176) rewrites Sartre, The Family Idiot vol. 1 (14142, tr. Cosman 1981; duplicate 14041), ch. 1 'A Problem', subsection 'Naïveté and Language' (six shingle runs of 8–17 words, one of 6; found by FTS '"weight of nomination"'). Acker turns Sartre's child Gustave into the 'he' beside a detective plot, cuts the names inside Sartre's sentences (Lacan's 'inarticulable'; 'the final vow of Saint Antoine—"to be matter."'; the Other → another person), changes single words (badly→poorly, unnamed→unnameable, given→GIVEN), inserts 'I want people to treat me as an animal', doubles 'To be matter. To be matter to matter.' This corrects day 2: McCarthy (4206, edge 40) calls the passage 'plagiarizing the magnificent climax of Flaubert's The Temptation of Saint Anthony'; only Sartre's three quoted words are Flaubert's (Hearn 13655: 'be matter itself!'). INWARD: Dworkin & Goldsmith, Against Expression (6336) reprint the GE opening (pp. 28–31) with a headnote naming Dickens and Guyotat and crediting 'plagiarism + pornography = autobiography' to Silliman (no other book in the library has the equation); 4 variants vs Penguin 2018 EPUB (text-layer gaps for old-style figures/small caps checked on page images). Myles, Pathetic Literature (4852) reprints all of Part Two 'Day: The First Days' (3,096 words), no headnote, with an eye-skip on 'living': 'If everything is living, it's not a name but moving. And without this living there is nothing' → 'If everything is living there is nothing'. Also noted, not checkable: the section opens a paragraph with Orlando's first sentence (Woolf not in catalogue). Edges 49–51.
nodes.carry_quote: “The word is never his; the trance soon absorbs the word, and by and by the word, fallen from the sky, oppresses him.” — Jean-Paul Sartre, The Family Idiot, vol. 1, tr. Carol Cosman, ch. 1, ‘Naïveté and Language’
prompts: 1. Acker removes the names inside Sartre's sentences (Lacan, Saint Antoine) and keeps their words; McCarthy puts one name back and gets the attribution wrong. Write a paragraph from a source of your own, removing every proper name but keeping the quoted words. Then give it to someone and ask whose it is.

2. The Against Expression headnote uses four verbs: appropriates, deforms, summarizes, rewrites. Take one page of your own writing that borrows from somewhere and mark each borrowed sentence with the one of the four that applies. Which verb has no instance, and why?
3. Myles's eye-skip removes 'it's not a name but moving.' Write the sentence that the omission has made true, then the one it has made false.

nodes.title: Shadow — Kathy Acker, day 5: Everything's Closing In
nodes.thread: Day 5 (who uses her without credit, suspected). (1) All 13 day-1 search terms, run through the calibre index with NOT Acker, return no book that lacks her name; the only hits are her own Great Expectations (1178) and books that name her (Myles 4852 reprint). Method caution: the index tokenises 'Acker’s' as its own word, so NOT Acker lets possessive-only books through (Green Girl 3597, Nace 3321, Private Novelist 11242 came back that way). (2) A read-only substring scan of all 12,668 text records in full-text-search.db for 40 of her most quoted lines and titles: 78 records match; 10 books outside Mentions, of which 8 are false positives (pirate histories for 'King of the Pirates'; Hölderlin and Benjamin's Early Writings for 'the childlike life'; heraldry; Sartre, her source; Myles, Not Me 4914, whose backlist prints 'Hannibal Lecter, My Father / KATHY ACKER' in capitals, missed by the day-1 capture; and 15020, this project's own Canetti-week compilation). (3) A 7-word-shingle comparison of 31 books by writers in or near her circle that never name her (Armand x13, Cooper, Myles, Kraus, Indiana, Lotringer, Kapil, Zambreno, Wojnarowicz, Heti, Valencia, Shields' Reality Hunger). SUSPICION (moderate): Louis Armand, The Garden (13051; notebooks 1994, Salt 2001, 11:11 Director's Cut 2020) carries 'already I can tell everything’s closing in on me' inside its single unpunctuated sentence (p. 132), followed by 'somewhere you’re repeating my too familiar phrases'; the sentence is the opening of My Death My Life, '1SEX', '4. War' ('Beginning: Already I can tell everything's closing in on me.'), and no other library book has it. Armand co-edited Pornoterrorism (10597, 2015), whose Vichnar chapter quotes MDML at length; The Garden credits Guyotat, whom Acker also rewrote (edge 32), and never names Acker. Weak: Clair Obscur (14221, 2011, p. 69) 'what if the sole purpose now is to get rid of meaning?' against MDML's '3VIOLENCE' heading 'Purpose: To Get Rid of Meaning'. (4) The uncredited use the scan actually proves runs outward again: MDML '2LANGUAGE', '3. Nominalism' rewrites Benjamin's 'Work of Art' essay (Zohn; library witness 1200): 'One might generalize by saying: the technique of reproduction detaches the reproduced object from the domain of tradition' verbatim, then her own gloss; Abel Gance cut from 'Presumably, without intending it, he issued an invitation to a far-reaching liquidation' (comma added). Armand's Solicitations (10595) quotes the same Benjamin sentence with credit. Also noted, not collated: MDML's Aeolus pastiche (Ulysses, 'HOUSE OF KEY(E)S'), seen through Armand's Joycemedia (13048). Run note: first attempt stopped when the Mac dropped off the bridge; completed on rerun the same day.
nodes.carry_quote: “already I can tell everything’s closing in on me somewhere you’re repeating my too familiar phrases” — Louis Armand, The Garden, p. 132
prompts: 1. Armand drops the full stop from Acker's sentence, and inside a book that is one unpunctuated sentence, the borrowed line becomes impossible to locate. Take a sentence you once borrowed and write the paragraph in which it would no longer be findable. What did you have to remove?

2. Acker keeps Benjamin's sentence about reproduction cutting the object loose from tradition, and cuts out the name of the man who 'issued an invitation to a far-reaching liquidation.' Write the line Gance would say if he could find himself in her paragraph.
3. 'Somewhere you're repeating my too familiar phrases.' Write two short paragraphs: one with Armand as the speaker, one with Acker. Which reading needs more evidence than The Garden gives?

nodes.title: Shadow — Kathy Acker, day 6: Slave Trader First
nodes.thread: Day 6 (the author again), run on 8 Nov in a weekend double with day 7 (7 Nov missed). Blood and Guts in High School (10951, Penguin 2017 EPUB) read whole, beyond the Grove pp. 34–37 band the critics quote. Finding: the inverse of GE/MDML. There she keeps sentences and cuts names (Lacan, Saint Antoine, Gance); here she keeps names and drops sentences. The book report names Hawthorne throughout, but 6-word shingles against The Scarlet Letter (Harvard Classics 5919) give 3 runs / 19 words; the only real one is the opening, with the women cut ('intermixed with women, some wearing hoods, and others bareheaded') and was→were; Dimmesdale's 'I charge thee to speak out the name' becomes the Reverend's abuse. Mr Linker recites Macbeth V ('a poor player That struts' → 'who struts') and the narration says 'Shakespeare said that in Hamlet': a misattribution given to the book's man of Culture (cf. McCarthy's Flaubert-for-Sartre, edge 40). The Propertius 'translation' ('Translating', 'On the desire for love') is a word-for-word crib of Elegies 1.1.1–16 in Latin word order (Loeb Classical Library Reader 5935, Goold, pp. 168–169): Cynthia→Slave Trader, Milanion→Psyche, puellam→the boy; contactum→diseased, castas→undiseased. Day 1 listed Propertius as not checkable; the Loeb Reader makes it checkable. Genet's Journal du Voleur quotation is unverifiable (Thief's Journal 1791 has no file). Coda: Janey's grave in the Saba Pacha cemetery 'in Luxor', then 'in Alexandria'. Edges 55–57 (all outward).
nodes.carry_quote: “because all books were written by dead people.” — Kathy Acker, Blood and Guts in High School, ‘The World’
prompts: 1. Element 2: Take four lines of a poem in a language you read and set English words under them in the original order, as Acker did with Propertius. Then change one name to someone in your own life. Which carries more of the original, the order or the meaning?
2. Element 4: Mr Linker gets the play wrong while praising Culture. Write a short scene in which a figure of authority misquotes, and make the misquotation the only true thing he says.
3. Write the acknowledgements page Acker never wrote, naming only the translators (Cosman, Zohn, Steegmuller, and the unnamed ones). Then list the translators your own commonplace book leaves out.

nodes.title: Shadow — Kathy Acker, day 7: The Translator Is the One She Leaves Out
nodes.thread: Day 7 (the map), same weekend edition as day 6. Graph of Shadow_Edges 29–57 (29 edges: Quotes 11, Rewrites 10, Argues with 4, Edits/introduces 2, Uses without credit suspected 2; 12 outward, 17 inward). Hub GE (12: 7 out, 5 in); BG 9 (3 out, 6 in); MDML 5 (2 out, 3 in; the only book with suspected uncredited users, Armand). Mentions: 265 rows, 261 non-own; 9 became edges (3.4%; Canetti 2.7%). Closing findings: (1) Of 12 outward sources, 5 reach her through English translators (Cosman's Sartre, Zohn's Benjamin, Steegmuller's Flaubert, an English Colette, a non-Fox Guyotat) and 1 through her own crib (Propertius); no translator is named in any of her four library books. On these shelves plagiarism becomes a question of translation. (2) Smallest-unit change holds at every remove: hers (eighty→sixty, Pip→Peter, was→were), her quoters' (this→the, room→bedroom), her editors' (eye-skip), her suspected borrower's (a dropped full stop), even her defenders' (Jenny, right wrist). Her method can't be told apart from what copying does anyway. (3) Names and sentences come apart: later books cut names and keep sentences; BG keeps names and loses sentences; the misattributions (McCarthy's Flaubert, Linker's Hamlet) sit where name and sentence meet. (4) No dissent in its own voice (day 3 confirmed). Limits: Empire, Don Quixote, Pussy not in catalogue; Thief's Journal has no file; nested-box tale in the BG coda (Setne?) unchecked; FTS timeouts. Next: Machado de Assis (Johnny's choice).
nodes.carry_quote: “because all books were written by dead people.” — Kathy Acker, Blood and Guts in High School, ‘The World’
prompts: 1. Five of Acker's twelve sources reach her through translators she never names. When she copies Cosman's Sartre, whose sentence is she copying? Write the paragraph that answers for one source you have used.
2. The library's copying of Acker drifts at the same scale as her rewriting. Copy one of your own paragraphs by hand without looking back, then compare. Is the drift yours or the paragraph's?
3. Nine of 261 mentioning books became edges. Choose one of the 252 that did not and write the edge you think is there.

nodes.title: Shadow — Machado de Assis, day 1: The Complete and Unabridged Gap
nodes.thread: Day 1 (the author). Dom Casmurro (1035), tr. R. L. Scott-Buccleuch, Peter Owen 2016 EPUB ('This complete and unabridged edition 2016'), compared chapter by chapter with the Garnier 1899 Portuguese (Project Gutenberg 55752). The 1992 cuts named by Krause (2015: ch. 52, most of 54, 55, first para of 56, 57–60, 63, 64) are restored; all 148 chapters present. But two passages are still missing and are not on Krause's list: ch. 98 'Five Years' loses its last two paragraphs (229 PT words: Escobar in coffee, the loan from D. Glória, Escobar as 'o terceiro na troca das cartas' carrying Capitu's first letter, his marriage to Sancha, 'sua cunhadinha', and 'Assim se formam as affeições e os parentescos, as aventuras e os livros'); ch. 73 loses the 67-word Alencar / Álvares de Azevedo citation. Scar in the English: ch. 106 'which is how he continued to refer to Capitu' refers back to nothing. Also: ch. 72's Portuguese Othello couplet ('Ella amou o que me affligira, / Eu amei a piedade della') replaced by Shakespeare's English. The 1991 introduction praises the book as 'easily accessible to the European and North American reader'; the surviving cut removes Brazilian literature. Mentions capture: 152 books (rows 609–760), by substring scan after the FTS call timed out. Brás Cubas (15092) and Memorial de Ayres (15091) added to the catalogue 10:30 UTC during the run.
nodes.carry_quote: “The fact is, everything is to be found outside a book that has gaps, gentle reader.” — Machado de Assis, Dom Casmurro, ch. 59, tr. Scott-Buccleuch, p. 103
prompts: 1. Ch. 98 ends in English on a man who once 'wanted to take his own life'; in Portuguese on 'as aventuras e os livros'. Write the last sentence of a chapter of your own twice: once closing on a person, once on books. Which makes the reader suspect the narrator?

2. Ch. 59 says everything may be supplied in a book with omissions. Write your own English for the omitted Escobar paragraphs without looking at a published version; then decide whether it helps Bento's case or Capitu's.

3. 'Lord Taciturn' against casmurro: four English words, each catching one part of the translator's gloss (gloomy, withdrawn, irritable, stubborn, sad). Which goes on the cover, and what does it decide before page one?

nodes.title: Shadow — Machado de Assis, day 2: The Butterfly on the Desk
nodes.thread: Day 2 (who quotes him). Seven books by five quoters, each quoting Brás Cubas through a translation not in the library (mostly Grossman, Epitaph of a Small Winner, 1952), checked against the 1881 Typographia Nacional text (Gutenberg 54829) and Jull Costa & Patterson 2020 (15092, from the 3rd ed.). The change is in where the sentence stands, not its words. (1) Murnane, A Million Windows (15095, section 19) remembers only the black butterfly of ch. 31 and moves it from story time (Tijuca, the next day; it lands on Brás's forehead, the windowpane, his father's portrait; 'inventor das borboletas') to the time of writing: it 'alighted on his desk' and took him for 'the god of the butterflies'. Stream System (3172) says what he was reading for: 'the writer’s way of interrupting his narrative'. (2) Booth, Rhetoric of Fiction (2180, epigraph to ch. VI, p. 148) quotes ch. 72 'The bibliomaniac' via Grossman; his ellipsis falls on 'e eu não quero dar pasto á critica do futuro': a critic cuts the critics. (3) Manguel, A Reading Diary (760, ch. 12) quotes ≥10 passages in his own versions: drops 'de graça' (the editor gives the definitive edition to the worms for free); Sandice → 'Stupidity'; in A Reader on Reading (1101) the same ch. 8 passage becomes madness invading 'our cellars' (Machado: sótão, attic). (4) Bartlett's (10410, credited to Grossman) prints Quincas Borba's Humanitist 'only one genuine misfortune: not to be born' (ch. 117) as Machado's maxim; Yale (2159, p. 510) prints 'fifteen months and three thousand dollars; nothing more' (PT 'onze contos de réis; nada menos') and the third-floor maxim of ch. 119, which the 1881 Brás says he tore up as unworthy of print. Edges 62–68. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “Just imagine: seventy years from now, a thin, sallow, gray-haired fellow, who loves only books, sits hunched over the preceding page to see if he can spot that nonsense.” — Machado de Assis, The Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas, ch. LXXII, tr. Jull Costa & Patterson (15092)
prompts: 1. Murnane puts the butterfly on the desk; Booth cuts the critics out of a passage about critics. Both make the novel more like what they came looking for. Write a page on a quotation that improves its source: is 'improves' a charge or a compliment?
2. Nada menos / 'nothing more': find a line you carry about that might have been reversed the same way, and check it against the original.
3. The 1881 Brás tears up his maxims; the later one offers them as epigraphs for 'speeches on no particular subject'. Which is the commonplace book's ancestor?

nodes.title: Shadow — Machado de Assis, day 3: Retreated from Brazilian Particularity
nodes.thread: Day 3 (who argues with him). The quarrel on these shelves is one argument about where his books live. (1) Schwarz, 'Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas', in Moretti ed., The Novel vol. 1 (1275, Princeton 2006, tr. Lubkemann Allen, pp. 816–840) is the only library text quoting Romero's Machado de Assis (1897) verbatim: 'the comedy of the almanac, the pessimism of ephemeral hack writing, which manages to delude those few simpletons who find it marvelous' (p. 819, n. 4 = Romero p. 160); an unnamed 'adversary' says Machado hid in 'peculiarly English' affectations. Schwarz argues with both camps: 'sympathizers and opponents were both of the opinion that Machado retreated from Brazilian particularity'; Veríssimo (n. 5) concedes the nationalist yardstick. (2) Jorge Amado, foreword to Rosa, The Devil to Pay in the Backlands (13307, Knopf 1963; signed Sept. 1962): Minas fiction 'has not yet freed itself from the apron strings of Machado de Assis ... a veritable model of polite phrasing'; Rosa 'Brazilian and universal at one and the same time'. (3) CHLAL vol. 3 (1261, catalogued as vol. 1): Skidmore p. 347 calls Romero's verdict (no memorable characters) 'least felicitous'; Moisés p. 83: Romero 1870 attacked the 'pretentious humor' of Falenas; Machado's 'A nova geração' (1879) answered. Machado argues back: third-edition preface (15092) answers Capistrano ('Is ... a novel?'; 'engraved goblet ... very different wine'); 1878 review of Eça as Zolaesque imitation (reported by Jull Costa, intro to 5839). Schwarz interview 1994 (7664): 'realist novels, but with antirealist techniques'. Detail: 1881 'Ao leitor' (Gutenberg 54829) lists 'um Sterne, de um Lamb, ou de um de Maistre'; later text (Jull Costa 15092; Schwarz from Aguilar 1959) drops Lamb; date of change not fixable in library. Edges 69–75. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “It is an engraved goblet, and while it may resemble the work of engravers of the same school, it contains a very different wine.” — Machado de Assis, Author’s Preface to the Third Edition, Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas, tr. Jull Costa & Patterson (15092)
prompts: 1. Schwarz says attackers and admirers shared one premise: state it in one sentence and look for it in your reading of Borges or Kafka.
2. Romero's 'simpletons who find it marvelous' against 'Ao leitor''s five readers: draft Brás Cubas's reply to Romero.
3. Lamb vanishes from the list of models: which influences would you cut from your own preface, and why?

nodes.title: Shadow — Machado de Assis, day 4: Psychiatrist, Find and Replace
nodes.thread: Day 4 (who translates, edits, introduces). The library holds three English books of O alienista (1882) but only two translations. The Melville House The Alienist (2012, 1138; EPUB names no translator; Wikipedia credits Grossman) is Grossman's The Psychiatrist (1963, in 4753) with the profession renamed: token comparison (~20,000 tokens, similarity 0.99) gives 100 psychiatrist→alienist, 'psychiatric doctrine'→'alienist doctrine', 'psychiatry'→'treatment'/'psychopathology', ellipses reset, OCR errors fixed; Grossman's footnotes kept. The renaming returns to Machado's word (alienista ×106; Gledson 14888: 'also translated rather anachronistically'; Jull Costa & Patterson 2483: alienist ×108) but keeps Grossman's freedoms: Father Lopes's threat to report Bacamarte 'ao papa' replaced by an invented joke plus a footnote on the pun (ch. II); ending 'no mesmo estado em que entrou' → 'as insane as ever'; 'nunca houve outro louco, além delle, em Itaguahy' → 'the only madman (in the vulgar or non-Bacamartian sense) ever committed to the asylum'; the rumour's reason inverted. Grossman's introduction transplants the four-fifths to Manhattan. Jull Costa & Patterson add a gloss ('also known at that time as alienism', ch. 1) and keep 'Casa Verde'. Oxford Guide (11676, p. 444): Scott-Buccleuch 'omits nine chapters' (cf. day 1). Polizzotti (6515, p. 150, via Thirlwell): Machado read Sterne in poor French translations. Edges 76–83. Portuguese: Papeis Avulsos 1882, Gutenberg 57001. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “The translator must also resist normalizing oddity, for Machado does sometimes say some very odd things.” — Margaret Jull Costa & Robin Patterson, Introduction, The Collected Stories of Machado de Assis (2483)
prompts: 1. Grossman cuts the Pope and footnotes the pun; Jull Costa & Patterson keep the Pope and drop the pun's second sense. Which loss is worse? Try your own English for 'pio trocado'.
2. 'also known at that time as alienism': footnote with its markers removed, or commentary posing as text? Compare Benjamin on the translator's task.
3. The Melville edition fixes the word and keeps the sentences. Sketch a theory of retranslation where the unit of fidelity is the sentence, and one where it is the term.

nodes.title: Shadow — Machado de Assis, day 5: Not in His Biographical Dictionaries
nodes.thread: Day 5 (who uses him without credit, suspected). Read-only substring scan of full-text-search.db (12,715 records, 63 strings from the day-1 list in four translators' English plus Portuguese; books containing 'machado' excluded). No borrowed sentence found in any book that never names him: Humanitism, Lord Taciturn, olhos de ressaca / whirlpool / undertow eyes, oblique gypsy, Life is an opera, Homer's cow, History of the Suburbs, two ends of my life, worm dedication, legacy of our misery, Bacamarte, Itaguaí, Capitu all null (null result recorded). What travels without the name is smaller: (1) Prince, Narratology (2975, 1982, ch. 4, p. 116, ex. 48) prints Brás Cubas ch. 72's opening via Grossman, credited only '(Epitaph of a Small Winner)': the same passage as Booth's epigraph (2180, p. 148, credited 'MACHADO DE ASSIS'), stopping where Booth's ellipsis begins; Prince cites Booth 'pp. 149-165'. Suspected relay from Booth, author dropped (moderate-high). (2) Almino, The Book of Emotions (2269): a Weimaraner named 'Quincas Borba' by a character 'who liked to quote left and right'; Machado never named: uncredited allusion (certain as reference). (3) Brooke-Rose, Thru (721, 1975): 'a small winner' ×2 and story 'Medium Losers and Small Winners' (via 2299); Grossman's title phrase (PT 'pequeno saldo'); weak. Irony: ch. 72's bibliomaniac 'Não conhece o autor'. Edges 84–86. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “He doesn’t know the author; the name “Brás Cubas” doesn’t appear in his biographical dictionaries.” — Machado de Assis, Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas, ch. LXXII 'The bibliomaniac', tr. Jull Costa & Patterson (15092)
prompts: 1. Prince keeps the sentence and loses the name; Almino keeps the name and loses every sentence. Which is closer to what Machado's bibliomaniac does with 'Braz Cubas'?
2. Booth's ellipsis cut the critic, and Prince's citation cut the author. Write the rule of quotation that would allow both cuts and forbid neither.
3. 'Small winner' belongs to Grossman, not to Machado. When a translator's coinage circulates uncredited, whose shadow is it in?

nodes.title: Shadow — Machado de Assis, day 6: The Thinking Erratum
nodes.thread: Day 6 (the author again). Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas (15092, tr. Jull Costa & Patterson 2020), read in the light of days 2–5 and collated with the 1881 text (Gutenberg 54829): the novel does to its sources what the week's quoters did to it — keeps the name, corrects, moves or cuts the sentence. (1) ch. XXVII: Pascal's thinking reed → 'a thinking erratum'; each season of life 'a new edition that corrects the preceding one' (cf. ch. XXXVIII 'fourth edition ... still infested with mistakes'); PT 'errata pensante'. (2) ch. CXLII: Quincas Borba, pointing at the page, quotes Pensées frag. 200 (Krailsheimer 7887) and moves 'the advantage' from the universe to man, then 'improves' it to hunger; JC&P 'rest of the world' for 'resto do universo'. (3) ch. CXLIX: Erasmus's mules (Radice 626) become 'dois burros', flattery becomes superiority, 'I will say what he did not'; Folly herself excuses the man who 'takes a donkey for a mule'. (4) ch. XCVIII: Pascal's l'ange et la bête (frag. 678) said to forbid 'simultaneous enjoyment'; de Maistre's 'soul and a beast ... on top of one another' (2031 ch. VI) is the closer model (suspected). (5) ch. XXV: Jaques quoted without Rosalind's 'good to be a post' (verified in 3396), the same cut-before-the-reply as Booth's ellipsis (day 2). (6) JC&P endnotes catch Machado's slips: Le Cid 'reversed (perhaps accidentally)', Tartuffe 'corrupted', Acts 9:7 'actually' 9:6 (1881 already '(Act., IX, 7)'); EPUB title 'que l'eût dit' vs 1881 'qui l'eut dit' unresolved. (7) Howard's introduction to de Maistre (2031, Mentions 631): Sterne → de Maistre → Machado, with Sainte-Beuve's Lamb (cf. day 3 'Ao leitor'). Edges 87–93. Read: targeted (~8% of chapters whole, all endnotes, intro, prefaces). No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “Pascal may say that man is a thinking reed, but he isn’t, he’s a thinking erratum.” — Machado de Assis, Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas, ch. XXVII, tr. Jull Costa & Patterson (15092)
prompts: 1. Brás calls man 'a thinking erratum' and Quincas Borba improves Pascal on the page he is pointing at. Is a misquotation that announces itself still a misquotation? Write the rule that separates Quincas Borba from Manguel.
2. Erasmus says the man who 'takes a donkey for a mule' is not mad; Quincas Borba takes a mule for a donkey and ends in 'semi-madness' (ch. CLX). Write the chapter Erasmus would add.
3. Jaques without Rosalind; Machado's ch. LXXII without its critics (Booth). Find a quotation in your own commonplace book that is famous only because its reply was cut.

nodes.title: Shadow — Machado de Assis, day 7: Name Kept, Sentence Moved
nodes.thread: Day 7 (the map). Graph of Shadow_Edges 58–94 (37 edges: Quotes 9, Argues with 6, Mentions 6, Translates 5, Edits/introduces 4, Uses without credit suspected 4, Rewrites 3; 9 outward from Machado's books, 23 inward, 5 between intermediaries). Hub Brás Cubas (17: 11 in, 6 out); O alienista 5 in; Machado as author/critic 5; Dom Casmurro 4; Grossman's Psychiatrist (4753) 4. Mentions: 152 rows, 143 non-own; 19 rows promoted (17 distinct titles; 13.3%; Canetti 2.7%, Acker 3.4%); 3 edges from books that never name him. New edge 94 today: Genette, Paratexts (692, tr. Lewin 1997) quotes 'To the Reader' (p. 291) through E. Percy Ellis 1955 (Additional references p. 414) and files it as a fictive actorial preface (p. 190): Ellis has 'a Sterne or Xavier de Maistre' — a third witness (with JC&P 2020) that Lamb, present in 1881 'Ao leitor', left the text later; 'puro romance' → 'pure romance' (genre becomes mood). Closing findings: (1) the shelves' Machado is a translator's Machado: ≥10 of 37 edges pass through Grossman (Epitaph, not held; The Psychiatrist, held twice); the only complete English Brás Cubas held (JC&P 2020) is quoted by no one. (2) The cut falls at the turn, where a text answers itself (Booth's ellipsis, Prince, Jaques without Rosalind, Scott-Buccleuch's ch. 98, Grossman's ending). (3) Three weeks: Canetti, the sentence travels and the concept does not; Acker, names and sentences come apart; Machado, the name is kept and the sentence moved, by him and to him. (4) The Brazil-or-world quarrel settled by the English editions against Brazil (Alencar cut, Othello in English, Manhattan, dollars). (5) The narratologists (Booth, Prince, Genette) take him at the threshold. Next proposed: Gérard Genette (Queue 7). No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “I wrote it with the pen of mirthful mockery and the ink of melancholy, and it is not hard to foresee what would result from such a marriage.” — Machado de Assis, Posthumous Memoirs of Brás Cubas, 'To the Reader', tr. Jull Costa & Patterson (15092)
prompts: 1. Ellis's 'pure romance' makes Brás's genre joke a joke about mood. Take a sentence of yours that names a genre, translate it into a language you half-know and back, and see which word goes false first.

2. The third-edition preface lets Machado correct Brás's list of masters without telling him. Write a preface for something of yours in which the author quietly removes one of the narrator's influences.
3. Genette's grid files Brás Cubas under one kind of preface. Draw the cell he left empty (the fictive preface-writer for a real author's book) and write the preface that would fill it.

nodes.title: Shadow — Gérard Genette, day 1: The Most Irritating Palimpsest
nodes.thread: Palimpsests (2356) theorises only 'the sunnier side' of hypertextuality, massive and declared derivation, and files undeclared borrowing ('plagiarism (in Lautréamont, for instance)') under intertextuality, refusing 'hypertextual hermeneutics'; the lost hypotext returns once, as Stendhal's Leuwen over Mme Gaulthier's vanished manuscript, 'the most irritating palimpsest of all' (ch. 78). The English book already carries layers: Prince's Foreword (whose sentences travel as Genette's in 133 and 12448), the translators' authorised excisions to the Appendix, and Borges quoted in an English (≈ di Giovanni) that differs from the library's Hurley (7517).
nodes.carry_quote: “one who really loves texts must wish from time to time to love (at least) two together.” (Genette, Palimpsests, ch. 80, p. 399)
prompts: 1. Genette refuses 'hypertextual hermeneutics' (p. 9) yet spends ch. 78 wanting a lost hypotext: when is not looking for a source a method rather than a lack?

2. 'every successive state of a written text functions like a hypertext in relation to the state that precedes it' (p. 395): describe one of your drafts in two states as hypertext of the first — transformation or imitation?
3. Three Englishes of Borges's swans (p. 252; 6623; 7517): write the fourth and name the operation you performed.

nodes.title: Shadow — Gérard Genette, day 2: According to Riffaterre
nodes.thread: Day 2 (who quotes him). Three books quote Genette word-accurately and still move the speaker. Allen, Intertextuality (3806, 2000): the ellipsis in 'The intertextual “trace” … is therefore more akin' removes 'according to Riffaterre' (Palimpsests p. 2), so Genette's report of Riffaterre becomes Genette's own 'analogy with the pictorial arts' (p. 98); a second ellipsis drops the hyper-/meta- parenthesis from 'text in the second degree' (p. 104 ← p. 5); the day-1 lost-hypotext passage arrives as 'Flaubert’s novel Leuwen' (p. 108; Genette p. 382 names Stendhal); 'both' dropped from p. 397. Boldrini & Novak (133): Ursula Hurley (ch. 11) credits Palimpsests in the body with 'massive and explicit palimpsestuous', a fusion of two Prince Foreword sentences; her note 27 credits Prince p. ix. Palazzolo (ch. 5, Paratexts p. 156 'mute gesture') and Alhambra Díaz (ch. 9, Narrative Discourse pp. 234–235, metalepsis; one comma) exact. Douglas, Frankétienne and Rewriting (12448, 2009): quotes the French Palimpsestes pp. 11–12 and glosses it with nine words of Prince's English Foreword ('grafting itself … onto a hypotext, an earlier text that it imitates or transforms'), uncredited (suspected). The declared quotation is where undeclared change happens. Edges 100–107. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “for the use of an epigraph is always a mute gesture whose interpretation is left up to the reader.” — Genette, Paratexts, tr. Lewin, ch. 7 'Epigraphs', p. 156 (692)
prompts: 1. Allen's ellipsis removes three words, 'according to Riffaterre', and keeps every other word true. Write a page on the ellipsis as an act of authorship: when does '…' assign a sentence to a new speaker?
2. Hurley's note is right and her sentence wrong. Is the footnote a confession the reader rarely hears? Write a paragraph whose notes contradict it and see which one the reader believes.
3. Douglas glosses a French quotation with someone else's English. Whose words do you think in when you think 'hypertext'?

nodes.title: Shadow — Gérard Genette, day 3: A Game of Chance, Like Roulette
nodes.thread: Day 3 (who argues with him). The library's arguments with Genette are about play, from two sides. Bell-Villada, Borges and His Fiction (13739, ch. 6 p. 134): 'Critics like Gerard Genette, in apparent disregard of Borges’s general spirit of humor and parody, have built entire theories on the fanciful notions played with in “Pierre Menard.”' (holds against Palimpsests p. 17 'succeeded in demonstrating'; not against p. 122's Menard joke, p. 253 'ironic detachment', or pp. 399–400 'Official humor is a contradiction in terms'; may date from the 1981 edition, before Palimpsestes). The Oulipo: Arnaud's protest (B.O. no. 63, not held) at Palimpsests ch. 9 p. 48 ('the Oulipism, like roulette, is a game of chance'; 'Chance is at the helm'; 'the Surrealist tradition'), reported by Levin Becker (777, quoted with the word order reversed) whose own definitions deny it ('not invested in … chance'; 'not an offshoot of Surrealism'; clinamen 'a voluntary breaking of a self-imposed rule'), and argued by Andrews (10153, ch. 4 pp. 98–99): 'drastically reductive', exercises confused with works; n. 7 the English p. 397 drops Queneau from the list of hypertextual moderns (verified English; French p. 449 not held); ch. 7 p. 192 Genette's oral 'a sad sort of play'. Doležel (6729) dissents from Fiction et diction (1991, not held; pp. 25–26), then translates Palimpsestes p. 435 himself (= English p. 384, 'method' for 'manner', widening clause cut) and uses 'régime ludique' against Foe's ideological critics (n. 29). The arguers end on the side of his play. Palimpsests re-OCR'd whole on the Mac (508 pp.). Edges 108–114. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “Official humor is a contradiction in terms.” — Genette, Palimpsests, tr. Newman & Doubinsky, ch. 80, p. 400 (2356)
prompts: 1. Bell-Villada says Genette built 'entire theories on the fanciful notions played with in “Pierre Menard.”' Name a theory of your own that started from a joke. Did the joke survive the theory?

2. Genette p. 48: chance 'cannot fail to turn into a re-creation'; the Oulipo: the clinamen is chosen. Write a paragraph in which the swerve is chosen by neither writer nor chance but by the translator (Queneau's name on p. 397).

3. Doležel's cut keeps 'in literature' and drops 'all second-degree artistic practices'. Write the gesture-theory version: can a gesture be hypertextual, or does Genette's restriction to texts stop it at the page?

nodes.title: Shadow — Gérard Genette, day 4: The Right to Be Unfaithful
nodes.thread: Day 4 (who translates, edits, introduces, rewrites him). Genette's only treatment of translation as paratext (Paratexts 692 p. 405: a translation 'revised or checked by the author' or self-translated (Beckett) has 'paratextual relevance'; n. 2 'the right to be unfaithful is an authorial privilege'; p. 264 n. 22 a translator's preface on her own translation 'ceases to be allographic'). The library's three English Genettes are made under three contracts: Narrative Discourse (5343, 1980) — Lewin 'silently modified the French edition ... correcting obvious errors', Proust in Scott Moncrieff except where 'Genette's exposition required a strictly literal rendering'; Culler: translation 'admirably clear', Genette's work 'testimony to the power of the marginal, the supplementary'. Paratexts (692, 1997) — Lewin: 'For the English translation, the author added a number of explanatory passages' (so by p. 405 partly authorial commentary; unmarked); masculine-pronoun rule her own; Macksey credits the translator in a parenthesis and gives Palimpsests to 'Channa Newman' alone (Doubinsky absent from 692). Palimpsests (2356) — examples moved to Appendix with approval (edge 96). Batchelor, Translation and Paratexts (7052, 2018) REWRITES the concept: Genette 'argues himself here into something of a corner'; new definition 'a consciously crafted threshold'; translation becomes 'a text in its own right and with its own paratexts'; does not test this on Genette's own English editions. Her Palimpsests quotations: epigraph cuts 'as one can see' (p. 4); p. 3 cited '33', ellipsis cuts 'taken within the totality of the literary work', bracketed glosses inside quotation marks; 'transcendance' for Macksey's 'transcendence'. Second English of Seuils intro: Maclean, NLH 22.2 (1991), not in library (via LexiconSE, unverified). Edges 115–120. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “But a commentary to be used with care, for the right to be unfaithful is an authorial privilege.” (Genette, Paratexts, tr. Lewin, p. 405 n. 2)
prompts: 1. Lewin: 'the author added a number of explanatory passages' — no list. Write the paragraph Genette might have added for English readers, and say what kind of paratext it is.
2. Batchelor's 'consciously crafted': name an accidental threshold (a catalogue error, an OCR) that changed how you read a book.
3. p. 405 n. 2 gives infidelity to the author alone. Where in your own rewriting would you claim it, and where deny it to your translator?

nodes.title: Shadow — Gérard Genette, day 5: Gerard Ginette
nodes.thread: Day 5 (who uses him without credit, suspected). NULL for sentences: every book that quotes his best-known phrases names him ('not only of transition but also of transaction' 13 books; 'vestibule' 6; 'fringe of the printed text' 5; 'Marcel becomes a writer' 8, the exception Kern 3535 (1970) predating Discours du récit). Coinages travel as common nouns without him (hypotext 11, peritext 5, metadiegetic 4, transtextual 27 'NOT Genette' hits); 'transtextuality' has other inventors (Rashkin via Castricano 9756; Watts on Conrad via Greaney 4688). What travels uncredited is the apparatus: Silva & Vieira, The Politics of the Book (6773, Intro pp. 5–6) quote Lejeune's 'fringe of the printed text which in reality controls one’s whole reading of the text' in Lewin's English, cited '(1975, 45)' to the French Pacte only = Paratexts p. 2 n. 5 (edge 121, suspected relay, moderate-high; Leary's 1989 English not checked); and give Genette's own p. 1 sentence ('a text to become a book and to be offered as such...') to 'McKenzie quoted in Genette 1997, 1' (edge 122, verified; McKenzie 12290 lacks it). Glass, 'Up from Underground' (Porn Archives 12079 ch. 6): 'paratextual packaging ... thresholds of interpretation', no Genette in the volume (edge 123, weak; reprint of Counterculture Colophon, not held). Method: credits invisible to search — 'Gerard Ginette' ×6 in Weaponising Speculation (5996, edge 124, Paratexts p. 319 n. 1 quoted, Lewin's 'Petit Robert' bracket moved to Alain), 'Gennette' (9365), letter-spaced 'ge ne tt e' (5196); FTS 'NOT Genette' passes 'Genette’s' with curly apostrophe (1136, 6505, 7332). Timeouts: proximization NOT Genette; who sees/who speaks; game of chance AND Oulipo; right to be unfaithful. No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “That had to be said in a note.” (Genette, Paratexts, tr. Lewin, ch. 12 ‘Notes’, p. 319 n. 1)
prompts: 1. Silva and Vieira credit Lejeune for words they took from Lewin. Write the citation a strict scholar would have given (Lejeune, as quoted and translated in Genette, tr. Lewin). Then decide whether that citation is more honest or only longer.
2. 'Gerard Ginette': a misspelt name keeps the credit and still makes it unfindable. Name a writer in your own reading whom you know under a wrong spelling, and what that spelling has cost you.
3. Genette on p. 319: 'That had to be said in a note.' Write a note that says something the main text could not have said.

nodes.title: Shadow — Gérard Genette, day 6: People Off to the Side
nodes.thread: Day 6 (the author again): Narrative Discourse (5343, Discours du récit 1972, tr. Lewin 1980), read for what days 2–5 found. It already contains the week's grammar: (1) the dropped relay has a name — Eucleides removes 'and I said' from the Theaetetus; Genette calls such forms 'reduced metadiegetic … or pseudo-diegetic' (pp. 236–237) = Allen cutting 'according to Riffaterre' (edge 100); (2) 'second degree' (p. 228 n. 41, metadiegetic) and 'threshold' ('a sort of threshold represented by the narrating itself', p. 228) begin as terms of narrative level, before Palimpsestes (1982) and Seuils (1987); (3) infidelity is first the reader's right ('totally unfaithful and wonderfully exact, like Pierre Menard', pp. 261–262) vs Paratexts p. 405 n. 2 'an authorial privilege'; (4) play is danger, not chance (metaleptic 'games', p. 235 n. 54; 'formidable game … also a dangerous one', p. 160 n. 97); (5) Lewin's notes narrate Genette in the third person ('In a note at this point Genette speaks of …', p. 27 n. 2), declare an omission (p. 94 n. 15) and leave other substitutions unmarked (Simms's Borges, p. 236 n. 55). Two carriers of the p. 236 sentence: Chamberlain 13682 (1990) quotes exactly and argues ('Metalepsis is unacceptable to Genette', p. 82; edge 126); Rabinow 1913 (2017, ch. 3 nn. 14–18) agrees and alters: Littré note given to the mood chapter (actually Intro p. 31 n. 9; cited p. 182), 'the' dropped and 'same' added, '[sic]' on an error not in Lewin, the rule of narrating given as the definition of metalepsis, 'puts' for 'put', 'perhaps' dropped, '[the same]' for 'some'; 3 of 5 page refs wrong (edge 125). Genette's own re-quotation of Proust's 'insincere language of prefaces and dedications' in Paratexts pp. 135, 231 (edge 129). No Candidates queued.
nodes.carry_quote: “the real author of the narrative is not only he who tells it, but also, and at times even more, he who hears it.” (Genette, Narrative Discourse, tr. Lewin, ch. 5 ‘Voice’, p. 262)
prompts: 1. Genette on the Theaetetus (p. 236): the 'and I said' is removed for the reader's comfort. Take a paragraph you have quoted from someone who was quoting someone else, and restore every 'and he said'. Then decide which version you would publish.

2. 'Totally unfaithful and wonderfully exact' (p. 261) is granted to the reader in 1972; 'the right to be unfaithful' is reserved for the author in 1987. Write the clause that would reconcile them, or the one that shows they cannot be.
3. Rabinow's '[the same]' looks like an editor's gloss and does the work of a rewrite. Write a sentence of your own whose meaning turns entirely on a bracket.

nodes.title: Shadow — Gérard Genette, day 7: The Old Analogy
nodes.thread: Day 7 (the map). The palimpsest has a source Genette stopped naming. 'Proust Palimpsest' (1961; Figures of Literary Discourse 6534, tr. Sheridan) ends on the figure and gives it, in n. 59 (p. 228), to 'this page from Baudelaire's Paradis artificiels, translated from the Suspiria de Profundis' — De Quincey unnamed ('quincey' 0 in 6534), his sentence reaching English through three hands ('ideas, images, feelings' → 'ideas and feelings'; De Quincey's English is in 8496). 'Principles of Pure Criticism' (1966, p. 72) calls the palimpsest his own, 'personal' 'critical desire'. Palimpsests (1982; 2356 pp. 398–399, n. 6–7 p. 471) calls it 'the old analogy', credits Amossy & Rosen (1974) and Borges's Menard; its English index lists Figures II, III, Mimologiques, ND, Palimpsests for Genette but not Figures I, and no De Quincey (edge 131, self-rewrite; index-based, French not held). The figure moves from one mind ('can only be deciphered together') to two texts ('love (at least) two together'). Neighbours: Borges 'Shakespeare's Memory' (7517) names De Quincey and turns his layers into 'text'; Manguel (1101) gives the sentence to 'Charles Baudelaire in 1869'. Edges 130 (Quotes), 131 (Rewrites), 132 (Logan, Edits/introduces). Map: 38 edges 95–132 (Quotes 17, Argues 5, Translates 4, Edits/introduces 4, Suspected 3, Rewrites 3, Mentions 2); Mentions 753, 12 promoted (1.6% of 747 non-own). Essay: the shelves' Genette is the second-degree Genette, his readers practise the 'sunnier side's' shadow, and he did it first to himself.
nodes.carry_quote: “Like Proust's writing, Proust’s work is a palimpsest in which several figures and several meanings are merged and entangled together, all present together at all times, and which can only be deciphered together, in their inextricable totality.” (Genette, 'Proust Palimpsest', 1961, tr. Alan Sheridan, Figures of Literary Discourse, p. 226)
prompts: 1. De Quincey's 'ideas, images, feelings' arrives in Genette's English as 'ideas and feelings' after three hands. Take a sentence you first loved in translation, find the original, and list what each stage removed. Then write the sentence the missing word would have made.

2. In 1966 the palimpsest is 'personal and therefore in no sense an exemplary one'; in 1982 it is 'the old analogy'. Write the paragraph in which a figure of your own (the gesture, say) stops needing your name. At what point does it?

3. 'can only be deciphered together' (1961) against 'love (at least) two together' (1982): simultaneity in one mind vs the pairing of two texts. Write a short piece, prose or verse, in which the two senses refuse to separate.

nodes.title: Shadow Week 8: New York School Poets
nodes.author: New York School Poets

nodes.title: The Anatomy of Melancholy
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: the cento. Compiling as cure; diagnosis of scholars' melancholy.
nodes.selection_logic: The largest cento in English, and the book most open about its own method, which it lays out in the preface. It supplies the diagnosis Flaubert dramatizes ('Love of Learning, or overmuch study', 1.2.3.15) and the method Mullen practises: recombining what has already been said.
quotes: “I write of melancholy, by being busy to avoid melancholy.” (Democritus Junior to the Reader)
“Omne meum, nihil meum, ’tis all mine, and none mine.” (ibid.)
“we can say nothing but what hath been said, the composition and method is ours only, & shows a Scholar.” (ibid.)
“we shall have a vast Chaos and confusion of Books, we are oppressed with them, our eyes ache with reading, our fingers with turning.” (ibid.)
“Many men (saith he) come to this malady by continual Study, and night-waking, and of all other men, Scholars are most subject to it” (1.2.3.15)
“I no sooner (saith he) come into the Library, but I bolt the door to me … in the very lap of eternity, amongst so many divine souls, I take my seat” (2.2.4.1, Heinsius)

nodes.title: Bouvard and Pécuchet
nodes.role_in_set: The copy: encyclopedic reading as comedy and disease; the Dictionary of Accepted Ideas as hinge to Mullen.
nodes.selection_logic: Burton's negative image. Two amateurs do the same encyclopedic reading, stupidity replaces melancholy as the subject, and keeping busy becomes the novel's engine. The Dalkey edition includes the Dictionary of Accepted Ideas, whose entries (MELANCHOLY, DICTIONARY, BOOK, LATIN) land on the other two books. Tagged priority_tbr.
quotes: “The pleasure they feel in the physical act of copying.” (ch. 11, Their Copy, plan)
“No time for reflection! Let’s copy! The page must be filled, the “monument” completed.” (ch. 12, plan)
“End with a view of our two heroes leaning over their desk, copying.” (ch. 12, plan)
“At the national library, they wanted to know the exact number of volumes.” (ch. 1)
“MELANCHOLY: Sign of a distinguished heart and an elevated mind.” (Dictionary of Accepted Ideas)
“DICTIONARY: Scoff at it—is only for ignoramuses.” (Dictionary)
“BOOK: No matter which one, always too long.” (Dictionary)
nodes.sample_highlight: Thus their last pleasure, their true, their sole pleasure was to resume, albeit fictitiously, that arid task which, for thirty-eight years, had been the occupation—and perhaps, without their knowledge, the happiness—of their lives.

nodes.title: Sleeping with the Dictionary
nodes.role_in_set: The dictionary: the reference work as partner rather than pathology; the emptied cliché.
nodes.selection_logic: Takes the reference book back from Flaubert's pathology. Mullen writes with the dictionary and thesaurus as collaborators, in alphabetical order. In 'Elliptical' she empties Flaubert's stock-phrase device and keeps only the frame. Like Burton's, hers is night-work.
quotes: “Any exit from the logic of language might be an entry in a symptomatic dictionary.” (Sleeping with the Dictionary)
“In the dark night’s insomnia, the book is a stimulating sedative, awakening my tired imagination to the hypnagogic trance of language.” (ibid.)
“The alphabetical order of this ample block of knowledge might render a dense lexicon of lucid hallucinations.” (ibid.)
“This dream is not a map. A poem is not the territory.” (Exploring the Dark Content)
“They just can’t seem to … They should try harder to …” (Elliptical)
“My honeybunch’s peepers are nothing like neon.” (Dim Lady)

nodes.title: Ethics
nodes.author_credit: Arnold Geulincx (with Samuel Beckett's notes; trans. Martin Wilson)
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor and source of the figure: the two clocks, the baby in the cradle, occasionalism as the ground of ethics (ubi nihil vales, ibi nihil velis).
nodes.selection_logic: The two-clock annotation (Ann. 19) gives the triad its image: correlation without causality, guaranteed by one artificer. The Brill edition prints it twice, once in Geulincx's text and again in Beckett's notes, which joins the axiom to Murphy and Molloy.
quotes: “It is the same as if two clocks agree precisely with each other and with the daily course of the Sun: when one chimes and tells the hours, the other also chimes and likewise indicates the hour; and all that without any causality in the sense of one having a causal effect on the other, but rather on account of mere dependence, inasmuch as both of them have been constructed with the same art and similar industry.” (Ann. to Tr. I, ch. II, sect. II, §2, Ann. 19, p. 232)
“I do not know how such a thing is brought about, and it would be impudent of me to say that I do what I do not know how to do.” (Tr. I, ch. II, sect. II, §2 [4], p. 33)
“Thus, I am a mere spectator of a machine whose workings I can neither adjust nor readjust.” (ibid. [8], p. 34)

“It is just like a baby laid in his cradle: if he wishes the cradle to rock it sometimes rocks, though not because he wishes it, but because his mother or nurse, sitting beside it, wills it” (Ann. 19, p. 232)
“the clock of my will and the clock of the world” (Ann. 48, p. 242)
“wherein you have no power, therein you should not will” (Ann. 3 to Tr. I, ch. I, §2, p. 178)

nodes.title: Speakable and Unspeakable in Quantum Mechanics: Collected Papers on Quantum Philosophy
nodes.role_in_set: The oblique edge: a physicist who meets the two-clock structure (egg and alarm clock; option 3, superdeterminism) and refuses it.
nodes.selection_logic: Bell's analysis of correlation versus cause restates the occasionalist problem without theology. Casimir's egg-and-alarm passage in 'La nouvelle cuisine' is the two clocks in a kitchen, and Bell's four attitudes after Aspect map what each book in the triad gives up.
quotes: “I want to boil an egg. ... Yet the coincidence of these two unrelated causal happenings is meaningful, because, I, the great chef, imposed a structure on my kitchen.” (paper 24, 'La nouvelle cuisine', §1, quoting Casimir)
“But apparently separate parts of the world become deeply entangled, and our apparent free will is entangled with them.” (paper 13)
“In such ‘superdeterministic’ theories the apparent free will of experimenters, and any other apparent randomness, would be illusory.” (paper 24, §10)
“In this matter of causality it is a great inconvenience that the real world is given to us once only.” (paper 12)
“the hands of the clock will have moved, and the moons of Jupiter.” (paper 12)
“How does the second sock know what the first has done?” (paper 16)
“Disgrace indeed, to be caught in a metaphysical position!” (paper 12)

nodes.title: Prince of Networks: Bruno Latour and Metaphysics
nodes.role_in_set: The lineage named and decentralized: occasionalism made secular and local ('vicarious causation'), where any actor can be the mediator and the bridge can fail.
nodes.selection_logic: Harman makes the Geulincx edge explicit (al-Ash'ari, Malebranche and the occasionalist tradition) and takes the monopoly away from God, custom or the mind. This gives the triad its conflict: one artificer, none, or many.
quotes: “This brand of philosophy, widely known as ‘occasionalism’, was as acceptable in the seventeenth century as it is ridiculed today.” (ch. 2, p. 35)

“Latour is probably the first thinker in history to invent a local option for occasional cause—one not passing through God (as in al-Ash’ari, Malebranche, and even Whitehead) or the human mind (as when Hume and Kant turn human habit or categories into the seat of all relations).” (ch. 4, p. 81)
“More occasionalist than Bergsonian, Latour’s actors have no choice but to occupy punctiform cinematic frames.” (ch. 5, p. 105)
“they allow a single pampered entity to break the ban on relations that is cruelly enforced on all others.” (ch. 5, p. 113)
“Bruno Latour is the first secular occasionalist” (ch. 5, p. 115)
“Custom is to Hume what God is to the occasionalists: the only genuine link between separate realities” (ch. 5, p. 115)

nodes.title: The Invisible Collection
nodes.role_in_set: Anchor: certification without an object. A blind collector shows blank sheets and points to collectors' stamps on their empty versos.
nodes.selection_logic: The purest case in the library of provenance outliving the work. It supplies the collector's marks (stamps, states, proofs, 'the Dresden copy') and asks what a connoisseur's description does when there is nothing left to describe. Its treasures are prints, already multiples, which is Krauss's and Benjamin's ground.
quotes: “he took out of the folio a mount framing a blank, yellowed sheet of paper, and held the worthless scrap out in front of him with enthusiasm.” (≈68%)
“his whole face magically expressing the intent gesture of a man looking at a fine work” (≈69%)
“there you see the stamp of the Nagler collection, here the stamps of Remy and Esdaile” (≈67%)
“to where the invisible collectors’ stamps that existed only in his imagination would have been” (≈72%)
“we put reprints or similar sheets of paper in the old mounts instead of the prints we had sold, so that he wouldn’t notice when he touched them.” (≈56%)
“Just promise me to draw up a handsome catalogue: it will be my tombstone, and I couldn’t ask for a better memorial.” (≈92%)
“‘Collectors are happy men.’” (last line)

nodes.title: Portrait of a Man
nodes.role_in_set: The object without its provenance: a forger with certificates for everything who cannot make an authentic Antonello, and finds his own face instead.
nodes.selection_logic: Inverts Zweig: certification is trivial ('They had them'), authenticity impossible. Winckler believes in the original enough to kill over it, which stages the conflict with Krauss from inside fiction. Antonello's cartellino ('me pinxit') is the self-certifying mark he cannot forge.
quotes: “to create an authentic masterwork of the past” (Part I, ≈31%)
“Anything by anybody of any period” (Part I, ≈66%)
“Forger. Faussaire. Fausse ère : wrong period.” (Part I, ≈83%)
“it was the double, triple, quadruple game of a fake artist pastiching his own pastiche” (Part I, ≈98%)

“I’d take three or four works by whomever, pick out various bits and pieces from them all, juggle them around and make a jigsaw puzzle out of them. But that didn’t work for an Antonello.” (Part II, ≈13%)

“‘And the certificate of authenticity?’ ‘They had them. I never knew where they got them, or whether they were fakes too or whether they had an official authenticator on their books.’” (Part II, ≈85%)
“I did succeed in painting my own portrait … I got my own face” (Part II, ≈88%)
“a painting cannot be a forgery and an authentic work of art at the same time” (Bellos, Introduction, ≈47%)

nodes.title: The Originality of the Avant-Garde and Other Modernist Myths
nodes.role_in_set: The theory both fictions test: the discourse of originality rests on a repressed discourse of the copy.
nodes.selection_logic: Names the certifying machinery Zweig's councillor points to ('the mark, the warrant, the certification of the original'), argues spontaneity is manufactured (Winckler's jaw, reversed), and starts from Benjamin on the print, the medium of Zweig's portfolios.
quotes: “we could say that all the casts of The Gates of Hell are examples of multiple copies that exist in the absence of an original” (p. 152)
“a legitimate work: a real original we might say” (p. 151)
“Sitting in the little theater, watching the newest Gates being cast, watching this violation, we want to call out, ‘Fraud.’” (p. 157)
“to find the mark, the warrant, the certification of the original” (p. 162)
“the modernist grid is, like the Rodin casts, logically multiple: a system of reproductions without an original” (p. 162)
“spontaneity was the most fakable of signifieds” (p. 167)
“we look back on the modernist origin and watch it splintering into endless replication” (p. 170)

nodes.title: Machines of the Mind: Personification in Medieval Literature
nodes.role_in_set: The machine described: the theory of personification as a tool of thought, with a typology keyed to the universals debate that places the other two books.
nodes.selection_logic: Gives exact terms for Folly (daemonic, 'faintly ridiculous') and Plume (nominalist puzzle); its opening persona 'Antonella', aggregated from data, is the mechanism Michaux later finds in his own self.
quotes: “personification is as personification does” (Intro, p. 9)
“Where novels often create an illusion of individuation through an accumulation of nonsignifying details, personifications are instead composed of exemplary or characteristic details.” (p. 2)
“it may be more accurate to think about it as a design engine, or even a form of artificial intelligence” (p. 4)

“nominalist personifications do not represent universals as much as they prompt readers to conceptualize them. They tend to be puzzles or enigmas, engaging readers through their incongruity rather than through visionary imagery or verisimilar detail.” (p. 24)
“Daemonic personifications, in contrast, are much less authoritative and can even be faintly ridiculous.” (p. 23)
“In later texts, it also illuminates the phenomenon of persons turning themselves into personifications.” (p. 25)
Excerpt pp. 5–6 (Gregory's machina)

nodes.title: Praise of Folly
nodes.role_in_set: The machine takes the floor: a personification delivering her own encomium, refusing definition, mocking the universals debate, and finally forgetting who she is.
nodes.selection_logic: Breen stops at the 14th century; Folly is what the device does next. A daemonic type who satirizes the realists and nominalists whose quarrel defines her, with a Psychomachia-like household turned into a court.
quotes: “It’s in praise of myself, namely, Folly.” (p. 11)
“Who could portray me better than I can myself? Unless, of course, someone knows me better than I know myself.” (p. 11)
“they still boast that they can see ideas, universals, separate forms, prime matters” (p. 85)
“so that you’d extricate yourself faster from a labyrinth than from the tortuous obscurities of realists, nominalists, Thomists, Albertists, Ockhamists and Scotists” (p. 88)
“But I’ve long been forgetting who I am, and I’ve ‘overshot the mark’.” (p. 134)

“When I wanted to play the fool, I assumed the character of Folly, and just as in Plato Socrates masks his face in order to sing the praises of love, I too have played my comedy in character.” (Letter to Dorp, p. 143)
Excerpt pp. 12–13 (refusal of definition)
“What shows such willingness to please as the way mules scratch each other?” (Folly's speech on flattery, before n. 87)

nodes.title: A Certain Plume
nodes.role_in_set: The machine run backwards: a particular who never becomes universal; the name thins into initials and the author declares the self an averaged persona.
nodes.selection_logic: The indefinite title stages the particular/universal problem; plume = pen, the writing tool personified, which then took over its author ('Votre Plume'); the 1938 Postface ('An averaged "self," a crowd movement') inverts Breen's persona machine.
quotes: “Extending his hands from his bed, Plume was astonished not to feel the wall: “Well, he concluded, the ants must have eaten it away. . .” And he went back to sleep.” (I, A Peaceable Man)
“Of the two it is always the object who’s in charge.” (XIII, Buddha)
“He who is firm is a man. But he who is soft is without limits. He takes on every form, he is born everywhere. Truth be told, he’s the Buddha.” (XIII, Buddha)
“Misfortune, my great plowman.” (XXX, At Rest in Misfortune)

“There is no single self. There are not ten selves. There is no self. SELF is but a point of equilibrium. … An averaged ‘self,’ a crowd movement. In the name of the many, I sign this book.” (Postface, 1938)
“not imposing enough or universal enough to assume outright allegorical significance” (Sieburth, Afterword)

nodes.title: Pause and Effect: An Introduction to the History of Punctuation in the West
nodes.role_in_set: The pause: the history, and the baseline claim that punctuation serves the reader. Source of the ¶ = C for capitulum link.
nodes.selection_logic: The floor under the other two: Szendy takes his history from it and Dames cites it on the ancient K. Its functionalism ('resolve structural uncertainties') is what the other two push against; its glossary joins the smallest mark to the largest unit. OCR scan; quotes checked against the OCR layer.
quotes: “Its primary function is to resolve structural uncertainties in a text, and to signal nuances of semantic significance which might otherwise not be conveyed at all, or would at best be much more difficult for a reader to figure out.” (Introduction, p. 1)
“such as a repertoire of intonations, or gestures and facial expressions” (Introduction, p. 2)
“the readers’ marks record individual interpretations of the texts.” (ch. 1, p. 14)
“the basic unit in a western text has been the paragraph or capitulum.” (ch. 7, p. 65)

“although every Reader hath a Right to point an ancient Author as he pleases, since the Art of Punctuation, if it may be so called, is of modern Invention, yet great Exactness is required when it is for public use.” (ch. 7, p. 91, quoting an 18th-c. editor of Horace)
“Laurence Sterne employs ‘elocutionary’ punctuation to enhance the intimacy between Yorick and the reader” (ch. 7, p. 92)

“A symbol developed from the letter C (for capitulum q.v.) with a vertical stroke, which largely replaced the paragraphus (q.v.) to indicate the beginning of a paragraph, proposition, stanza or section” (Glossary, paraph, p. 305)

nodes.title: Of Stigmatology: Punctuation as Experience
nodes.role_in_set: The point: punctuation as the blow that makes experience and exercises power; the long reading of Tristram's cut.
nodes.selection_logic: Contradicts Parkes while borrowing his history; its Sterne chapters are the center of the triad, and its claim that punctuation includes 'chapter breaks' hands the question to Dames. Lacan/Derrida on the point de capiton.
quotes: “For punctuation is never merely a matter of style or rhetoric in the common sense: It is force; it is power; it is political decision.” (p. 2)
“The sensations, the events, that strike or dot me must be marked, punctuated, for me to have lived them.” (p. 2)
“Punctuation as the doubling blow, as the singular flash or clap that, remarking what happens, allows us to have and to inscribe an experience of it.” (p. 4)

“Besides the punctuation of sentences, there is what literary theorists call the punctuation of the page or work. The concept of punctuation thus overflows itself in all directions, since it ends up including blank spaces as well as chapter breaks” (p. 5)
“Far from being able to anchor anything or anyone somewhere, the button point is unbuttoned.” (p. 22)
“A subject that one can thus think, in the image of Perekladin, as at once punctuated and punctuating” (p. 31)
“opinion itself is not a matter of opinion, far from it: It is a construction that is a matter of a technology of pointing and punctuation.” (p. 101)

nodes.title: The Chapter: A Segmented History From Antiquity to the Twenty-First Century
nodes.role_in_set: The chapter: the largest regular cut as a technology of lived time; Sterne's staircase as the image of the break.
nodes.selection_logic: Answers Szendy without the violence ('traversable' ruptures) and shares ground with Parkes in the early history of kephalaia and capitula. Puts gesture at the break ('The break occurs midgesture'). Table 3.1 charted.
quotes: “This is a book about ruptures. But traversable ones: gaps one crosses, fissures within continuities, the marks within an individual life.” (Ante Chapter, p. 3)
“Where that unit is not already marked or summarized, it can be summoned into being by the reader’s own gestures.” (ch. 2, p. 63)
“the kephalaia are not unities but instead incitations” (ch. 3, p. 92)
“For Locke, chapters are the artifacts of communal approaches: citation, proscribed ritual segmentation, numbing serial interruptions.” (ch. 5, p. 149)
“The break occurs midgesture” (ch. 5, p. 161)
“The chapter is a pause on a step or landing, a continuing motion or gesture caught midway, the awkwardness of stopping somewhere one is meant to keep traversing.” (ch. 5, p. 163)
“Our comprehension of time is continually and inescapably punctuated and divided, not only in retrospect but in the very moments of its formation.” (Post Chapter, p. 290)

nodes.title: Observations upon Experimental Philosophy (extract: 'sky' sections)
nodes.year: 1666 (2nd ed. 1668); file is a 15-page bilingual éditions Clinamen extract
nodes.role_in_set: The philosopher's refusal: the glass deludes; natural eye plus regular reason.
nodes.selection_logic: 'Of Telescopes' argues the case the other two dramatize: sight works only within 'a certain proportion of distance betwixt the Eye and the Object', past which a glass gives pictures, not natures. The flight section adds the shared frame: 'Art cannot give new motions to natural parts'. Note: the file is only a 15-page extract (four sections), not the Cambridge edition the record describes.
quotes: “how these actions are performed inwardly, no Microscope is able to give us a true information thereof.” (Of the Celestial Parts, p. 6)
“put the case, the Moon, or any other of the Planets, were inhabited by animal Creatures, which could see as much of this terrestrial Globe, as we see of the Moon” (p. 5)
“Man is apt to run into extreams, and spoils Nature with doting too much upon Art.” (Of flying, p. 4)
“whether it be onely a delusion of the glasses, I will not dispute” (Of Telescopes, p. 8)
“I chose rather to follow the guidance of regular Reason, then of deluding Art.” (Of Telescopes, p. 8)
Excerpt: 'Of Telescopes', opening, p. 8

nodes.title: Gulliver's Travels
nodes.role_in_set: The satirist's answer: abolish the lens by resizing the observer; Gulliver becomes the instrument.
nodes.selection_logic: Brobdingnag turns Micrographia into lived experience (skin with 'great Holes', lice with snouts); Laputa keeps the instruments and loses the world. The edition's note names Hooke's fleas and flies as the target, so the triad's absent centre is named inside one of its books.
quotes: “I could see distinctly the Limbs of these Vermin with my naked Eye, much better than those of an European Louse through a Microscope; and their Snouts with which they rooted like Swine.” (II.4)
“I should have been curious enough to dissect one of them, if I had proper Instruments (which I unluckily left behind me in the Ship)” (II.4)
“whose large Opticks were not so acute as mine in viewing smaller Objects” (II.3)
“the Stumps whereof they plainly discovered through a Magnifying-Glass” (II.3)
“although their largest Telescopes do not exceed three Feet, they magnify much more than those of a Hundred with us, and shew the Stars with greater Clearness.” (III.3)
“So that I really began to imagine my self dwindled many Degrees below my usual Size.” (II.3)

Editor's note: “unpleasant picture of enormously magnified insects was possibly intended as a satire on such members of the Royal Society as Robert Hooke, whose Micrographia (1665) contained some striking micrographical illustrations of fleas and flies” (Explanatory Notes, II.3)
Excerpt: II.1, the skins passage

nodes.title: Lady Macbeth of Mtsensk: Selected Stories of Nikolai Leskov ('The Steel Flea')
nodes.author_credit: Nikolai Leskov (trans. William Edgerton for 'The Steel Flea')
nodes.year: 1881 ('The Steel Flea'); Edgerton trans. 1969; NYRB selection
nodes.role_in_set: The craftsman's answer: skill surpasses the instrument, invisibly and unsigned, and the improvement stops the flea dancing.
nodes.selection_logic: The instrument is real but English and renamed in skaz as a 'nitroscope'; the Tula smiths outdo the flea without it ('we just sharpened our eyes'), and the English diagnose what the victory cost. The story prompted Benjamin's 'The Storyteller', which brings hand and craft into the triad.
quotes: “coming down to the hidebound flea, which you can’t see with your eyes but can only feel when he bites you between your hide and your body.” (§3)
“he took the flea and put it on his tongue and said, “I feel something cold, like strong metal.”” (§4)
“Because I did smaller work than these flea-shoes,” he said. “I made the nails the shoes were fastened on with, and they are too small for any nitroscope to blow them up.” (§14)
“We are poor people—too poor to own a nitroscope, so we just sharpened our eyes.” (§14)
“you didn’t realize that such a little machine as the one in the nymphusoria was calculated for the most accurate exactness, and it can’t carry the flea-shoes.” (§15)
“machines have evened up the inequalities in gifts and talents, and genius no longer strains itself in a struggle against diligence and exactness.” (§19)
Excerpt: §13, Lefty's method ('look one at a time at each foot it walks on')

nodes.title: Arioflotga
nodes.role_in_set: The incipit as the whole book: 4,108 first lines of a lost anthology, alphabetized, no poems behind them.
nodes.selection_logic: The purest case in the library of Flannery's 'book that is only an incipit'. Alphabet replaces plot; the phantom country Oblivia (91 lines) supplies a ghost literature; two lines pastiche Hesiod and Genesis, Jullien's Western openings. Title = initials of 'A Revised Index Of First Lines Of The Great Anthology'.
quotes: “I have only had glimpses of the life I would like to have had.” (epigraph)
“A,b,c,d and so on. Where’s the problem?” (first line, under A)
“At first, in the beginning, there was no such thing as Time.” (under A)
“All poets fail. That is, perhaps, what poetry is.” (under A)
“I can’t get these bloody openings out of my mind.” (under I)
“Let me, I beg you, O Muse, begin this epic about poetry,” (under L)
“No actual poem anywhere would begin like this” (under N)
“Zzzzz. No, no. Don’t wake me up. In fact,” (last line, under Z)

nodes.title: If on a Winter's Night a Traveler
nodes.role_in_set: The theory of the incipit as narrative promise; ten broken-off first chapters; Flannery's wish for a book that is only a beginning.
nodes.selection_logic: Flannery's diary (ch. 8) states the fascination, the wish and the copyist's vocation; ch. 7 gives the counter-view that every first line refers to something already begun, which is the hinge to Jullien. The ten titles form one unfinished sentence (ch. 11).
quotes: “I would like to be able to write a book that is only an incipit, that maintains for its whole duration the potentiality of the beginning, the expectation still not focused on an object.” (ch. 8)
“it is the promise of a time of reading that extends before us and can comprise all possible developments.” (ch. 8)
“Everything has already begun before, the first line of the first page of every novel refers to something that has already happened outside the book.” (ch. 7)
